# Localization Strategy for an Adaptive-Learning Platform
## "Same Learning Promise, Different Classroom"

---

## 1. The core diagnostic

Four failure modes kill US edtech companies in these markets, and they are all versions of the same mistake — treating localization as a content problem.

**Translation is not localization.** A Vietnamese fifth-grader and a French CM2 student are not doing the same maths in a different language. Topic sequence, notation, expected solution methods, and what counts as a correct explanation all differ. A translated US item bank produces content that is linguistically correct and pedagogically illegitimate — which teachers detect within one lesson.

**Curriculum is a legal artifact, not a market preference.** In Kenya, curriculum-support material must be vetted by KICD before it can enter a classroom. In Vietnam, core-subject content must align to the 2018 national programme and typically ride an approved publisher. In Saudi Arabia, content sits inside a state system with ETEC/MoE standards and a values review. In France, resources reach schools through ENT/GAR plumbing, public procurement, and a CNIL-shaped data doctrine. You do not "enter" these markets; you get **admitted** to them, on a 9–18 month clock.

**Procurement determines the product, not just the sales motion.** A ministry buys a *platform it can control and populate*. A Vietnamese parent buys an *exam score*. A French collectivité buys a *teacher-directed, RGPD-clean resource with a French pedagogical warranty*. A donor buys a *cost per verified learning gain*. These are four different products wearing the same logo. If you build one and sell it four ways, three markets reject it.

**"Attitudes to screen time" is a trust problem, not a UX setting.** French resistance to screens and to algorithmic profiling of children is a political and professional position, held most strongly by the teachers who are your gatekeepers. Streaks, leaderboards, and "engagement minutes" — the exact metrics that win in Vietnamese D2C — are disqualifying signals in a French staffroom.

**The resolution: hold the *learning promise* and the *engine* constant; let the *curriculum, the pedagogy shell, the trust envelope, and the commercial motion* vary.** Every market gets the same claim — measurable mastery gains, evidenced against *that country's own* assessments. Nobody gets the same product surface.

---

## 2. Six-layer architecture, with a hard fork rule

| Layer | Contents | Variation policy |
|---|---|---|
| **L0 — Engine (invariant)** | Learner model, mastery inference, item selection, spaced retrieval scheduler, psychometric calibration, content pipeline, offline sync, identity, entitlements, analytics | **Zero forks.** Single codebase, all markets |
| **L1 — Curriculum graph** | Canonical language-neutral skill ontology + prerequisite DAG; per-country **standard overlays** and sequencing | Data, not code. One overlay per country |
| **L2 — Content & items** | Locally authored or licensed items, explanations, worked examples, reading passages, media | Fully local. Native-authored, never machine-translated into production |
| **L3 — Pedagogy shell** | Feedback style, motivation model, session length, testing framing, teacher/parent surfaces, gamification on/off | **Pedagogy Packs** — declarative config bundles |
| **L4 — Trust envelope** | Data residency, DPIAs, child-data rules, content-safety policy, accessibility, approvals, AI governance | Per country, legally reviewed |
| **L5 — Commercial motion** | Packaging, pricing, channel, contracting, support | Per channel, not per country |

### The Localization Ledger (the discipline that keeps this from fragmenting)

Every local request is classified before any work starts:

- **Class C — Configuration.** Expressed as data or feature flag. No platform engineering. **Target: ≥85% of all local requests.**
- **Class E — Extension.** A plug-in at a published seam: payment adapter, SIS/ENT connector, auth provider, assessment exporter. Approved by the platform team; the *interface* must be reusable even if the implementation is single-market.
- **Class F — Fork.** Divergent core logic or schema. Requires Localization Board approval, a named owner, a **sunset date**, and a merge-back plan. **Hard cap: three live forks globally.**

Two supporting rules: nothing enters L0 unless it serves **two or more markets** or is a compliance requirement; and any Class F item still open at its sunset date is either merged, generalised into a Class C capability, or the market feature is withdrawn.

---

## 3. The curriculum graph — the single most important design decision

Build **one canonical skill ontology** (language-neutral atoms with prerequisite relationships) and treat every national curriculum as an **overlay** mapping official standard codes → canonical skills, with its own grade placement and sequence.

Consequences worth stating explicitly:

- **The learner model, adaptation logic, and telemetry pool globally** even though no content is shared. A Kenyan learner's fraction-equivalence evidence improves item-selection priors used in Riyadh, without a single item crossing a border.
- **Reporting renders in local codes.** A French teacher sees *socle commun* language; a Kenyan teacher sees CBE competencies; a Saudi supervisor sees national standards. Same underlying object.
- **Coverage and gap reports become a sales asset.** "Our overlay covers 94% of the Grade 6 programme; here are the 6% we do not yet cover" is far more credible to a ministry than "fully aligned."
- **Difficulty does not transfer.** Item parameters must be recalibrated per language and population — use shared priors, local posteriors. Claiming transferable calibration is the fastest way to lose psychometric credibility with ETEC, KNE

In 2026, an adaptive-learning startup is expanding from the US into Vietnam, Saudi Arabia, France, and Kenya. Each country mandates different curricula, language-of-instruction rules, and attitudes toward foreign educational content; parents and teachers hold different beliefs about screen time and standardized testing; and government procurement processes differ from direct-to-consumer purchasing.

Design a product strategy for localizing an adaptive-learning platform across countries with mandated curricula, different parental attitudes, and mixed procurement channels, balancing a shared technology core against local fit.
